utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we resume to hear the evidence of Trifunovic, there are a couple of matters to deal with on the part of the Chamber. First, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on whether time limits should be imposed on the Prosecution's cross-examination of witnesses called by the accused. The Chamber recalls that on the 12th of November, 2012, following a lengthy cross-examination by the Prosecution, the accused's legal advisor asked the Chamber to consider imposing limits on the time spent by the Prosecution on its cross-examination. On the 14th of November, 2012, having heard 21 Defence witnesses, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to make oral submissions in relation to the time it spent on cross-examination. In doing so, the Chamber noted that overall, the Prosecution used significantly more time than the accused on examination-in-chief and re-examination combined and that for the majority of witnesses called by the accused, the evidence presented pursuant to Rule 92 ter was extremely limited, consisting of short statements, very few associated exhibits, if any, and a limited number of issues discussed. On the 15th of November, 2012, the Prosecution responded in short that it has demonstrated commendable efficiency in that, number one, there is not necessarily a link between the length of a statement or the number of associated exhibits sought for admission under Rule 92 ter and the length of cross-examination; number two, it has drastically reduced its already "relatively modest time estimates" and has ended up spending much less time than anticipated; and, number 3, it has used the same percentage as that used by the accused on cross-examination during the Prosecution's case while the accused is using practically no time when tendering evidence under Rule 92 ter. The Chamber notes that the accused did not wish to respond to the Prosecution's submission. The Chamber first wishes to recall that during the Prosecution's case, it started imposing systematic time limits on the accused's cross-examinations from the 11th prosecution witness onwards. The Chamber has now heard 24 Defence witnesses and considers it has sufficient information on the basis of which to consider whether the imposition of time limits is warranted. Turning now to the Prosecution's argument. First, the Chamber does not accept that there's no link between the volume of Rule 92 ter evidence sought for admission and the necessary length of cross-examination, nor is the Chamber satisfied that the Prosecution has demonstrated efficiency in conducting cross-examination by maintaining the same ratio as that used by the accused during the Prosecution's case. On the contrary, there should be a correlation between the amount of evidence sought for admission and the amount of time necessary to rebut it. The Rule 92 ter packages for the first ten witnesses called by the Prosecution contained between two and eight days of testimony in addition to a substantial amount of time used for live examination and a large number of proposed associated exhibits. In comparison, as stated earlier, for the overwhelming majority of witnesses called by the accused thus far, the Rule 92 ter packages have been very limited. The Prosecution argues that when the statement is limited or when few or no associated exhibits are sought for admission, it is for the Prosecution to reconstruct the background during cross-examination. The Chamber does not consider that this is the function of cross-examination. The Chamber simply cannot comprehend why it would take more time to rebut information which is not sought for admission than to rebut vast volumes of evidence. The Prosecution's point that cross-examination is shorter when more evidence is tendered in examination-in-chief does not hold. On repeated occasions since the start of the Defence case, the Chamber has warned the Prosecution on cross-examination that it should move on to the next question and has also questioned the necessity of some of the questions asked. I would refer here as non-exhaustive examples to transcript pages 28694 and 28970 from the date of 17th of October, to 29159 of 22nd October, and 29255 of 23rd of October. In relation to the Prosecution's argument that it has drastically reduced its already "relatively modest time estimates" and has ended up spending much less time than anticipated, the Chamber considers that the time estimates have been far from modest and disagrees with the argument that they show that the Prosecution has been extremely efficient in conducting its cross-examination. Thus on the basis of all the reasons that I have referred to earlier, the Chamber considers that the time has come to impose limits on the Prosecution's time for cross-examination. As it did with the accused, the Chamber will endeavour to inform the Prosecution of the time it has for cross-examination sufficiently in advance of the witness appearing before the Tribunal. The Chamber will consider the scope of anticipated testimony, type of witness, quantity and type of written evidence proffered for the witness, if any, number of associated exhibits tenders, if any, the Prosecution's requested time for cross-examination, and to a lesser extent the accused's estimate of time for examination-in-chief. Furthermore, as it did with the accused, the Chamber is amenable to giving additional time upon showing of good cause. In order to assist the Chamber in its assessment of time required for cross-examination, the Chamber would once again remind the accused of the necessity to provide accurate and timely Rule 92 ter notifications, in particular when it comes to associated exhibits sought for admission. That being said, for the sake of notice, the Chamber will not impose any limits for the next witness after Miladin Trifunovic, namely Velimir Dunjic. For the remaining witnesses for the week, the Chamber hereby informs the Prosecution that it will have one and a half hours for Mile Sladoje, one hour for Zoran Kovacevic, and one hour for KW318 -- K318. In light of the pending motions for exclusion, or partial exclusion, of evidence of witnesses Angelina Pikulic, Branislav Dukic, and Radojka Pandurevic, the Chamber is not yet in a position to determine time limits for cross-examination. It will inform the parties in due course. Next, the Chamber refers to the accused's motion to admit evidence of Milorad Krnojelac pursuant to Rule 92 quater, filed on the 15th of October, 2012, and the Prosecution's response to that motion filed on the 29th of October, 2012. After having reviewed the motion, response, and related materials, the Chamber would like to ask for some clarification from the accused about a couple of issues which arise from this motion. Mr. Robinson, the Chamber understand that Mr. Krnojelac was on the original Rule 65 ter witness list which was filed on the 27th of August, 2012, and was listed as witness number 262 to testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Following the Chamber's instruction that the accused considered the relevance and potential repetitiveness of some of the 579 witnesses listed on this initial witness list, the Defence filed the supplemental submission pursuant to Rule 65 ter and a revised list of witnesses on the 11th of September, 2012. The accused specifically represented that he had "taken on board the Trial Chamber's comments as to the relevance and repetitiveness of some potential witnesses" and that he had dropped ten witnesses from his 65 ter list. As per footnote 3 of the September notification, one of the only ten witnesses dropped on the purported grounds of relevance and repetitiveness was witness number 262, which was Mr. Krnojelac. In light of these observations, so, Mr. Robinson, can you confirm that Mr. Krnojelac was originally dropped from the accused's 65 ter witness list on the grounds of relevance and repetitiveness, and then when the Defence was informed that he had passed away, it proceeded to file a motion for the admission of his 595-page transcript of testimony in the Krnojelac case itself. So the Chamber would like you to also clarify when exactly you learned of Mr. Krnojelac's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We learned of his death in between the filing of the first and second Rule 65 ter submissions, and we took him off the list once we learned of his death. We probably should have made it more clear that he was being dropped for a different reason than the others, but we lumped them all together. And after we learned that he had died, we just took steps to take him off the witness list and began to review his testimony to see -- in his own trial to see whether a 92 ter quater motion should be filed and then when -- after we had done that, we filed that motion. So he was not dropped for reasons of relevance or repetitiveness. And I apologise that we didn't make that clear in the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a different perspective, could you tell us why there is a good cause for the Chamber to grant leave for Mr. Krnojelac to be added back to the 65 ter list given the chronology of the filings that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't believe that a Rule 92 quater witness necessarily should be on the witness -- Rule 65 ter list, and you'll see that none of our Rule 92 quater witnesses are on that list, and we had filed all of our motions before the witness list was filed and it didn't include those witnesses. So I believe we do need good cause to show why we didn't file that motion by the 27th of August when the Rule 92 quater motions were due, and the good cause that we are asking you to consider is the fact that we didn't realise that Mr. Krnojelac had died. That's why we put him on the witness list as a live witness on the 27th of August when we -- someone called it to our attention when they saw him on the witness list. We checked it out and found out that in fact he had died, so we believe that constitutes good cause for allowing us to have a variance from the dead-line for Rule 92 quater witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Off the top of my head and speaking for myself, I have difficulty following your submission that for the Rule 92 quater witnesses they shouldn't -- it is not necessary for them to be included in 65 ter list. Do you have any basis for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Rule 65 ter list, as far as we understood it, was for witnesses whose evidence would be offered subsequent to the 27th of August, and so as a result, we only included all of those who we actually anticipated from the time forward would be witnesses. We didn't -- as you see, we didn't include any of our Rule 92 quater witnesses for whom motions had already been filed. So in other words, we basically believed it was redundant to put witnesses on a witness list for whom motions had already been filed for admission and who were deceased and therefore wouldn't be appearing before the Chamber. If that's -- there may -- I don't know if there's jurisprudence on this issue as to whether 92 quater witnesses have to be on the Rule 65 ter list, but I could research that if you'd like, but that's the basis upon which we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Tieger, on the issue of this Rule 92 quater motion? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not based particularly on the jurisprudence, Mr. President, just based on what I've just heard in court, but two things occur to me. Number one, even assuming for the sake of argument the rationale presented by Mr. Robinson with respect to the earlier witnesses for whom motions were simultaneously pending, many if not all of which ultimately denied, I don't see how that would apply to the Krnojelac situation. That's two different circumstances. And number two, I wish I could say I was surprised by the assertion that it was only after Mr. Krnojelac died that the Defence decided to review his statement, but I'm not. That is a matter that I will allude to further at some point during the course of the day and in connection with some other information I have to bring to the Court, but I think that also tends to undercut the strength of the Defence's position on this matter, their own assertion that it was not until such time as they learned of the witness's death that they felt it would be useful to know what it was he might have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we read Rule 65 ter, subparagraph (G)(i)(e) which says: "An indication of whether the witness will testify in person or pursuant to Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 quater by way of written statement or use of a transcript of testimony from other proceedings before the Tribunal." I think it's clear. Well, I'll leave it at that, and unless there's other matters to deal with, we'll bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll have a matter that I think takes more time than we should use at the moment. I'll raise it perhaps at the beginning of the next session, but I did want to inquire before we begin in light of the Court's earlier comments concerning the issue regarding interview of Defence witnesses by the Prosecution, that those -- the Court considered that to be a bit of a storm in a teacup, I wondered whether the Chamber wanted us to address the accused's recent motion for clarification orally so we can move quickly on this matter one way or another. We can do it written -- in a written manner if the Court prefers or I can respond now. But that was my only inquiry. Or I could respond later in the day if the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, I just saw the filing and I didn't read it. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. I think in light of the arguments that were made previously, the motions and the decision that this is really a motion for reconsideration cloaked as a motion for clarification. First of all, the accused is now asking for something that he specifically asked for previously. Indeed, that was alluded to in paragraph 7 of the Court's decision, and the Court did not grant it, clearly. Secondly, the accused's motion -- or his efforts in this regard thus far have been based on a kind of alleged need for parity. The Prosecution did not seek in the previous -- when the situation was reversed did not insist on, ask for, or allude to the need for the Defence to do anything other than let us know. In fact, I don't even know that we specified that because that was based on the jurisprudence. We just asked when the Defence wanted to contact witnesses for whom they had contact details already that they identify themselves clearly so that the witness would know who was talking to them. Third, the Court's decision is clearly grounded in two basic principles. Number one, there's no property in a witness; and number two, it's a matter of professional courtesy to let the other party know that you intend to speak to the witnesses. That's exactly what we did. If the Defence wishes on that basis, then, to take steps to contact their witnesses either first or afterwards, they're free to do so, but we've complied with the order. The order is clear, and it's -- it's rounded on the principles that I just identified and no further steps need be taken. And finally, I should note that the Defence alludes in a couple of places in their motion to the alarm that witnesses might feel. Let me say quickly two things about that. Number one, it seems to be a highly speculative and fanciful argument, but number two, to the extent that the Defence is indeed concerned about alarming witnesses, it seems to be because there are many witnesses who have never been contacted by the Defence in the first place to know that they are witnesses, and I -- and the Defence actually sent us a letter asking us to provide them with the contact details of the witnesses we intended to contact, which certainly indicated to us they had never been in contact with those people and didn't have their contact details and their concern about raising any alarm with witnesses is based on the fact that that would be the first time apparently that these witnesses knew they were to testify in this case. That's a problem created by the Defence entirely. It shouldn't change the basis for the Court's order, and we think there's -- as I say, this is -- there's no need for clarification, and to the extent the motion is instead a motion for reconsideration in another guise we ask that it be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you like to add anything to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. After your order, the Prosecution sent us a letter indicating they wanted to interview 210 witnesses for whom they had contact details and 309 witnesses for whom they didn't, for whom the Victims and Witnesses Unit would need to make the contact and for whom we would have to provide contact details for them. So virtually our entire witness list was returned to us by the Prosecution as indicating these are the people they would like to interview. Subsequently, the Prosecution advised the victim witness section it wasn't necessary to contact the 309 witnesses that they would be conducting the great majority of the interviews here in The Hague and that they could be contacted prior to their coming to The Hague or when they arrive in The Hague to make those arrangements. But for the 210 witnesses that they have contact details for, now they don't want to specify to us which ones they actually plan on interviewing. So we have to contact all of those witnesses pursuant to the order, or we would like to contact all of those witnesses, and we don't think that that's really a wise use of our resources, and also it would -- because it can cause concern among people who don't need to otherwise be concerned because the Prosecution will probably interview a very small percentage of those witnesses. So we're spinning a lot of wheels and causing a lot of concern and angst that don't need to be done. We propose and we think that what the Court had in mind was a more targeted approach, that if the Prosecution generally intends and wants to interview a particular witness let us know. We'll immediately contact the witness and that will be the end of it, and they can go ahead and make contact with the witness directly. This way, everybody's working on things that actually have to be -- are productive instead of spinning wheels that don't need to be spun, and that's our point, and that was the point of our request for clarification, because your order indicates that if the Prosecution wishes to contact a Defence witness, then this procedure should be put in place where we're given the opportunity to contact them first. So we're asking you to clarify the meaning of wishes. Is the wish some abstract desire that some day maybe under some circumstances they might possibly decide they want to talk to the witness or is it something that's more focused that they actually do have a firm intention of wanting to speak to that witness, and that's the issue before you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You referred to a concern on the part of the witness. What kind of concern would there be if the Prosecution wishes to interview the witness himself or herself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would imagine the fact that many of our witnesses particularly in the municipalities portion of the case were themselves either suspects when interviewed by the Prosecution the first time or are concerned about possibly being prosecuted in the state court in Bosnia as a result of their usually -- role on the Crisis Staff in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to protract this argument to any great degree, Mr. President, but I need to indicate that this is, in our submission, a complete deflection by the Defence. Mr. Robinson is aware that we wish to interview those witnesses, and the reason we wish to interview them is because in large measure we haven't been provided with any meaningful information about them. So another matter I wish to raise today but not at this moment, because of the time that's passed. In other words, it's the Defence that created this situation in the first place by not complying with Rule 65 ter (G), not providing the information we needed. They're very much aware of fact that that underlies in large measure the need to talk to all these people. It certainly could be the case that if we ever received proper information and the information to which we're entitled under the Rules that some of these witnesses might not need to be interviewed. That's number one. Secondly, with regard to wheel spinning, again that's a matter that's been created by the Defence. Had they met with these witnesses in advance, it would certainly have been appropriate to tell those people, You may be contacted by the Prosecution, certainly up to you one way or another whether you wish to talk to them, we leave that matter to you, et cetera, et cetera, as is commonly done. Nor would they have any need to turn to the Prosecution for the contact details of people they listed on their witness list without providing any information whatsoever, any meaningful information whatsoever about what those people would testify to. And second if there's any wheel spinning that's entirely up to the Defence. If they wish to contact those witnesses they can, pretty much in short order if -- to simply advise somebody that they may or may not be contacted by the Prosecution. To that extent this is a storm in a teacup. The -- back to the Chamber's original decision it dealt with that. It considered the accused's earlier request to have this kind of power over when the Prosecution would speak to people and which people they'd speak to based on what action the Defence might take and the Court rejected that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider the matter and issue a ruling in due course. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to put on the record that Witness KW492 will not be called. He was scheduled to be called this month but after learning of the Trial Chamber's decision concerning his protective measures, he has refused to testify in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I continue to ponder why Mr. Robinson feels it necessary to put these -- this matter on the record. There are a million reasons why witnesses don't want to testify. We raised that matter the first time that Mr. Robinson attempted to do this and identify some of the factors that we considered led to the witness's decision not to testify. I think this is a transparent attempt to suggest a necessary link between the trial's decision and put pressure on the Trial Chamber with regard to its decisions regarding protective measures and I consider it to be inappropriate and I'm going to ask that it cease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. Robinson, I tend to agree with Mr. Tieger's observation, but -- and further, I don't think it's an appropriate way of using court time. So in the future, if necessary in your opinion, would you put that in writing. Well, let's bring in Mr. Trifunovic. Shall we move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think going into closed session may -- yes. We need to draw the blinds. Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trifunovic. I apologise again for your inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, during the past 11 days since you left the courtroom, have you spoken to anyone about what you had testified about?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And have you spoken to anyone about the evidence that you may be about to give?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one except my family. My family knew that I was returning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you didn't discuss any -- any detail in relation to any evidence you may give?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions about the function of the commander of the Vogosca Brigade. Your statement doesn't actually say when you became the commander. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially the 20th of September, 2002, by the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was when you were -- you received formal written notice, but it's right, isn't it, that you been performing this function as the commander of the Vogosca Brigade for some time prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the Blagoje [as interpreted] Battalion because it was the strongest battalion, and there were no active-duty officers, and my role was to unify these battalions until someone came there, one of the professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When -- when did you become commander -- I'm sorry, just for one moment. In your answer, you said officially the 20th of September, 2002, or that's at least how it's in the record. Did you mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. I believe that's the date. Perhaps I may be off by a couple of days, but I believe it's in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So when did you become commander of the Blagovac Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before the war in peacetime in the former Yugoslavia I was a TO commander of a unit in Blagovac which was charged with defending Pretis. That unit was deployed in Blagovac, and its sole role was in the event that it was necessary and that the factory which was nearby was under threat, the role was to defend that factory, Pretis, and since that's how it was, then I just remained as part of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who appointed you to the function of commander of the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was appointed through -- when an official document was issued, and I was appointed by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Informally, who appointed you to be the commander of the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall every detail, it was a long time ago, but I believe it was the Vogosca municipality, the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. There were two municipalities that were established then, one was Serb and the other Muslim, and I was appointed the commander of Vogosca Brigade by that side. That was my task. I was entrusted with this task until Colonel Vukota arrived who then established the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Colonel Vukota you're referring to as -- do you mean Colonel Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So getting back to your appointment by the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, who actually are we talking about? Can you name the people that appointed you informally to the position?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rajko Koprivica was the president of the Executive Committee and there was also Svetozar Stanic, who was president of the Assembly, the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know what Jovan Tintor's role was. He was a member of some fora [as interpreted]. I don't know what exactly he did. He was involved in political life, but he was not in the municipal -- in any of the municipal bodies at that time. I know that he was later appointed, but what he was doing at that time exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did he have any involvement in the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at first I don't remember what that was called. A Crisis Staff, a Municipal Staff, something like that. Well, anyhow, he was top political leader. What he did exactly, I don't know. I don't know what his role was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago Colonel Vukota Vukovic appearing on the scene in around May, and you stated in paragraph 7 of your statement that this Tactical Group was formed from the Vogosca, Ilijas, and Rajlovac Brigades and that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He was the commander of the Tactical Group that included the Vogosca, the Kosevo, and the Rajlovac Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you also aware that in September General Galic issued a formal appointment forming an Operational Group from the units of Ilidza, Ilijas, Igman, Rajlovac, and Vogosca Brigades and that Vukovic was its commander?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that really. This is the first time that I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But as commander of the Vogosca Brigade, you reported daily and sometimes more to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command from May through December, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as needed we reported. When the Tactical Group was established, then most of that went through the Tactical Group, because the immediate -- my immediate superior unit was the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you were sending your daily combat reports to the command copying the Operative Group; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sent daily reports for the most part to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because that was the system in place. They were in the field, so they didn't have any equipment or means to receive them. So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to talk with you now about your arrest in December 1992. I want to clarify a couple of matters. You were asked about your arrest and detention at transcript pages 30372 and 30375. What was the date you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the 14th or the 15th of December, if I'm not mistaken. I believe it was the 15th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a group of officers arrived, and there were also some political figures with them at the time, the mayor -- I may be mistaken because I don't know all the names and functions of the people, but the mayor, Trifko Radic; Ratko Adzic, who was the president of the municipality; and the then president of the municipality, Rajko Koprivica; the military police, the corps military police, they came and arrested me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So Koprivica was from the Vogosca municipality. Trifko Radic and Ratko Adzic, can you just tell the Chamber which municipalities they were from?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trifko Radic was from -- or Ratko Radic from the Ilijas municipality, and Trifko Radic was the mayor of all the municipalities in the area of the Serbian Sarajevo as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said the corps -- SRK corps military police arrested you. Can you just very briefly tell us the circumstances? Where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when they arrived, and I believe it was around midnight, I was at the command headquarters at the brigade command, my brigade, and I had just gone to sleep, and I thought that they had come to discuss the situation which was very alarming, especially in Zuc because there had been intense fighting. The Muslim forces were trying to get through to Vogosca. So they pushed us back all the way back to Gola Brdo and 850 elevation, and we stopped there in order to fortify our positions because there was no place else where we could go. All the fighters who were on that front line were fighters fighting outside their own homes and some 150 metres or so, 30 to 150 metres behind them were their families. So they came to my command then, and they said that I was guilty of losing this elevation or trig point 850 because we had lost some 100 metres, we as a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that -- this is at transcript page 30372, that you were detained with four of your assistants and all the leadership members of the Rajlovac Brigade. The four assistants that you're referring to, do you mean Kenic, who was the deputy of the brigade and your Chief of Staff, Momcilo Kenic? Was he arrested with you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Milan Terzic, Captain Milan Terzic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Major Sretko Skipina?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who else from the Vogosca Brigade was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so who were the leadership members of the Rajlovac Brigade who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Rajlovac Brigade there was the president of the municipality. Bozic was his last name, but I can't recall his first name. And the entire command of the Rajlovac Brigade, Simatovic -- I can't recall all the names, but I believe there were 17 of them or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who replaced you as the commander of the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on whose orders, but I believe that some people from the Ilijas Brigade were appointed such as Bosnjak, warrant officer Bosnjak, and this was on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then who took over after him?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After him? Well, I don't know if I'm going to guess the order right, but I believe he was followed by Major Robert Jovanoski, an active-duty officer, but he didn't stay there long. Then Major Antic came, but he didn't stay long either, and then Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] until the brigade was formed including these three brigades, the Ilijas, so the Rajlovac --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the last person you mentioned? Lieutenant-colonel who?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Milos Delic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After your few days of detention, you then took up duties as commander of the Blagovac Battalion, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that didn't happen soon. I was on leave for the situation to settle down, and then I took over the role of the Blagovac Battalion commander. I can't recall the date, but it was in 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you stayed in that post up until the end of 1993, early 1994, when you became the transport manager at Pretis?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as commander of the Blagojevic -- Blagovac Battalion, you reported to the commander of the Vogosca Brigade, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, I want to deal briefly with the matter we would -- we left off at last Thursday. We looked at orders which were issued by you for the detainees to be used in the field and at Zuc. You saw that the War Commission, Vogosca War Commission, was copied on some of the orders. It was your habit to keep the Vogosca War Commission informed of your orders and requests such as these for prisoners to be taken for work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show it to me. I don't know what we are exactly discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P05999.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This was -- this was one of the orders that I showed you last Thursday, and we see here that it's an order to take prisoners for work at Zuc, and we can see that the War Commission's copied; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it here in my language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can scroll the page up, the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see it there? If I can show you another document. Do you see that there, Mr. Trifunovic, where it says copying the prison administration and the War Commission and then a copy for the files? Do you see that on that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can we also have Exhibit P06000, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can see down the bottom again. This is an order for you for prisoners for work at Zuc, and we see it's sent to the prison administration and the War Commission in the file. So my question -- but I asked you before we looked at these exhibits if it was your habit to keep the War Commission informed of your orders and requests such as these, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't standard practice. I don't know why they were copied here. I no longer remember. In any case, the War Commission did exist under the heading of Nikola Poplasen, at least for a while, so perhaps this was during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 18 that each soldier and officer in your unit was informed on several occasions of the orders issued in relation to the prohibition of opening fire on civilians and civilian facilities. How did you inform your subordinates of this?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oftentimes we had briefings, perhaps daily or every couple of days depending on the situation and the ability to attend. During the briefings all problems were discussed, individual units and their issues, et cetera. We tried to come up with solutions for those problems in the best possible way so as to avoid any repetition of such problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. There is an important element that is missing. He said if there were cases such as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you confirm saying that, Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I said that there were briefings, perhaps daily which depended on the situation, and every unit or unit commands discussed their problems in the field. We tried to come up with solutions to those problems and to issue tasks accordingly to tackle them in the best possible way if there were such cases with undesirable effects. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said also in that paragraph that opening fire on civilians and civilian facilities was only allowed if the unit's security was seriously compromised. What do you mean only if the unit's security was seriously compromised?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it in the statement I drafted or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's P02444, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be provided with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's coming on the e-court. Can you take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraph -- no, no. No. D, sorry, D.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraph 18. So what did you mean by only if the unit's security was seriously compromised?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please allow me to finish with my reading and then I can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. May we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, have you read that paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you mean by only if the unit's security was seriously compromised that you could open fire on civilians and civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently the Muslim forces made use of civilian facilities as their strongholds in order to deploy mortars and store artillery pieces which they used against us. It often happened in the area of Menjak. They used the houses there as strongholds to engage in sniping or artillery attacks in order to target the gate of the Pretis factory while the workers disembarked from the buses, and we had many wounded and killed workers. In such cases, we tried to eliminate such sniping or mortar positions by neutralising them in order to prevent any further fire. We believed that fire was coming from civilian houses. We didn't know whether there were civilians there or not, but we could clearly see that we were engaged from such locations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add something. The witness said that there were many killed workers and many wounded workers. Line 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Civilians, workers, and anyone who passed by. That was the main route. In order to avoid such incidents and in order to avoid engaging such positions, we placed metal containers so as to block the view from their machine-gun nests so that they wouldn't be able to see people coming on the buses, and we tried to preserve the lives of workers and passengers in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The -- it was reflected that witness said that we had many wounded and killed workers. I think it was already reflected. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And not knowing whether there was civilians in those buildings or not, you engaged in those -- firing on those locations.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not locations but individual houses with fortified cellars from which we were being attacked, having many wounded and killed people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move on to another topic, and that is you said that you knew that there were aerial bombs and that they appeared in the second half of the war, and that's in paragraph 19 of your statement. And you said that you were told of the G14 incident which relates to a modified air-bomb being allegedly fired from Pretis towards Dositejeva Street in Sarajevo on the 16th of June, 1995. Who told you about the G14 incident?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard it on the news, on the Muslim TV and radio that a shell had been fired, or whatever they called it, from the location of Pretis. They called it a modified projectile. As far as I recall, I have never seen such a bomb, an air-bomb, and I don't know what it looks like. I also don't remember any firing from that location. Having in mind the size of that bomb, we should have been able to hear the detonation, whereas I did not, I have not. That was sometime during the war, and people were saying that there were such things, but I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You weren't in the brigade at that time in June 1995, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the brigade, but I was in the factory within the perimeter of the Pretis factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware that in June 1995, specifically on the 15th of June, 1995, that the Vogosca Brigade had a launcher for an aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, there was no Vogosca Brigade. There was only the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. Now, whether as part of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade there were such bombs or launchers as some call them, that's something I don't know. I've never seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. The Vogosca Brigade did -- was renamed into the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade at some point. I want to deal now with the last topic, and I have a number of documents that I wish to show you, and if we can move through this as briefly as we can because we have some limited time. You said in your statement that: "There were several paramilitary units in Vogosca municipality, and the civilian authorities, with our help and support, kept taking steps to get rid of these paramilitaries because no unit wanted to include them in their ranks." And you said that in paragraph 21 of your statement. Which paramilitaries are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that's how things were at the beginning of the war. There were many paramilitary units. There were self-proclaimed commanders until things fell together. There were units and volunteers who came from elsewhere who refused to be placed under the command of the VRS. And if -- in case they refused to, we strove to get them out of our area, to have them eliminated from the area because they were causing more harm than good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, which paramilitary units were these? What are the names of the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their names were. There were volunteers, paramilitary units with all sorts of nicknames. I can't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll give you a few names. What about Boro Radic's group?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Radic did have a unit of his. He refused to be placed under military command, and then he was issued some separate task perhaps by the Tactical Group or someone else, but I think he acted independently most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When Radic's group first came -- first of all, what was the group made up of? Where did this group come from?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Radic, if I recall him well, hailed from Vogosca. He was married to a Muslim lady. Initially in 1992 he was a member of the Patriotic League. He created some kind of joint Patriotic League but then there was a rift --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- following which he brought some unfamiliar people from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 2366, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a list dated the 25th of May, 1992 - that's Exhibit P02366 - and it's a list of names 22 men in the special detachment, and the first one on the list is Boro Radic. Who did these men report to in -- in May 1992: Jovan Tintor, the Crisis Staff, you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never reported to me. I had no co-operation with them whatsoever, and we were not in contact, at least not in any positive meaningful way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What crimes did Boro Radic's group commit in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was neither a security officer nor a MUP officer who would be tasked with gathering such information. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear about any of the crimes he was -- his men were -- he and his men were committing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I heard and whatever I did not see is something that I'm not competent to discuss. I don't know. I wasn't in any of the crime scenes following the crimes that were committed, if there were crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you and the civilian authorities were trying to get Boro -- were trying to get these paramilitary groups out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 24172, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is dated the 27th of June. It's a request for the issuing of a vehicle to a member of Radic's special unit. And this is the War Commission who is giving this person a Golf. Is this the same local authorities that you were talking about who were trying to get rid of Radic's group?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. There were no others. Second of all, there was no War Presidency, and anyone could put anything in writing. I don't know. This was not sent to us. I don't know who it was sent to, and I have no idea if it was approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the men from Boro Radic's special group incorporated into units within the Vogosca Brigade in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. When Boro Radic was killed, I don't know what month that was, perhaps in August. In any case, the group, the unit, fell apart. Some returned to their home units -- or, rather, to the units where they were supposed to belong, whereas others left. I don't know anything else. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 01631, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, this is a document from the VRS Vogosca Brigade command dated the 30th of September, 1992, and it's an order. If we can go to page 2 and page 3 in the B/C/S. This was an order which was signed, I think, by your deputy, the Chief of Staff, Kenic, disbanding Radic's group. It's signed on your behalf as commander of the Vogosca Brigade, and it puts the units within the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The 30th of September, 1992. And if you compare this document with Exhibit P02366, if you compare the names in both of those documents, you can see that there are a number of names that are the same. For example, if we can go back to page 1 of this document, this document on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us show him the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we put up P02366 on one -- on the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and in the B/C/S, and the B/C/S remains of 65 ter number 01631 on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see in the 1st Company four names: Branislav Josipovic, Ljubomir Tosovic, Zivorad Markovic, and Nebojsa Trifunovic. And those four names appear in the exhibit on the right-hand side which is P2366, do they not? If we go to the 2nd company, you'll find item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's hear from the witness. The B/C/S translation takes time. Yes, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered. While Boro Radic was alive, who had been known to the criminal investigation police, he gathered that group and refused to be placed under the command of any unit. As soon as he was out of the picture, these people asked to be joined with any of the units in the brigade area. They asked to be placed under military command. Some of the personnel from his unit left the territory of Vogosca since they did not want to be placed under military command. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we go to the 2nd Company, you'll find item number 4. Boro Jovicic also appears on the other list as well. And if we go to the last list of names in the English version, which is the brigade's Reconnaissance Platoon -- or in fact in the B/C/S version, you'll find numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 also appear on the list. If we can go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't need the Exhibit P2366 any more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. Oh, well, yes, if he wants to compare the names or, in fact, their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very difficult if you refer to English page then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I said B/C/S, Your Honour. I corrected myself. If we can go to the -- yes, there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You can see that numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 also appear on the right-hand side of the screen. So you agree that this group of Radic's special detachment soldiers have been incorporated into the Vogosca Brigade by your order of the 30th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you weren't trying to get rid of them, were you, if you were incorporating them into your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but they had been established as some sort of unit. Now, whether they were within the Tactical Group or something, I don't know. I don't know. As soon as Boro Radic was no longer there, we made an effort to have all people return to units that wished to be placed under the command, because we did not have enough manpower, enough resources, nothing. Every soldier who was willing to place himself under the command was welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one -- two other areas that will take me about seven minutes. I would think seven to ten minutes, but I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- we'll have a break for half an hour, and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender the last two documents, 65 ter number 24172 and 65 ter number 01631, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any objection to 01631, but as far as 24172 is concerned, the witness didn't confirm anything about that document and it doesn't directly impeach or contradict his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, I tend to agree with Mr. Robinson's observation, but if you would like to respond with respect to 24172 I will hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it go to the general impeachment of this witness in relation to him saying that it was him and the civilian authorities who were wanting to get these people out of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think, yes, the Chamber agrees with that. On that basis, we'll admit that, both of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 24172 will be P6001 and 65 ter number 01631 will be Exhibit P6002.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, another paramilitary group which was in the Vogosca municipality was the Sosa Detachment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a detachment which was -- which was under Jovo Ostojic's command, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, once this detachment came into Vogosca for a few days, they did not want to place themselves under the command, and they sort of got lost. I mean, if I understand correctly who this is about, we tried to eliminate them from the area, and then they left and where they went I really have no idea, but they didn't stay there for a long time. I think they are some sort of paramilitary unit, I don't know, but they did not stay long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where did this paramilitary come from? They came from Serbia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were some kind of volunteers. Now, where they came from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This detachment was paid by the Bosnian Serb authorities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on which basis they came and whether someone paid them or did not pay them, whether anybody paid them. I don't know. I just know that this group came. That was probably their name. They didn't want to place themselves under the command. They didn't want to hold the defence lines. They were not interested in that, and we saw them off, let them be of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P05418, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 28th of July from Koprivica, who was president of the Executive Board of the Serb municipality of Vogosca, sent to the War Commission, and it's giving approval for the -- stating, sorry, that approval had been given in principle by representatives of the Vogosca municipality to remunerate volunteers engaged under the command of the Jovo Ostojic. Now, you said that this group just came on one occasion and then they disappeared. Does this document refresh your memory as to whether they were engaged in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in our area for a few days. I've already said that. And then when they got this area of responsibility to hold the line at Zuc, they didn't want to do that. And then I disassociated myself from them. Now, where they went after that and what they did afterwards, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P02377, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 30th of July, 1992. It's a war commission conclusion about paying the Sosa Detachment under Major Jovo Stojic's command saying they were indispensable for the successful defence for the municipality of Serbian municipality of Vogosca. Are you sure you don't recall these -- this detachment being in Vogosca for more than a few days?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that we, since there were far less of us on our side than there were soldiers on the other side, each and every soldier was welcome as far as we were concerned. Whoever came and placed himself under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska was welcome. These people were there for a few days and left. Now, where they were put up, I don't know. If I can remember this properly, they were there for a few days, and then after that they went to some other area, I guess. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A few days when? In -- in what month?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably in this period. I mean, I don't know. I cannot remember each and every date. I mean, this was 20 years ago. Probably in this period that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have Exhibit P02373.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We see this is dated the 15th of July, 1992. It's from Stanisic, who you mentioned earlier in your testimony today as president of the Serb municipality of Vogosca, writing to the Ministry of Finance of the Serb Republic of BiH requesting to be reimbursed of cash funds for monies paid out from the 1st of April, 1992, to the 14th of July, 1992, to brigades and also 500.000 dinars for Serb volunteers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that, but I didn't know about any of this. I mean, which way they were paid or whether they were paid. I mean, I just know they didn't stay for long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. So I think you said they came for a couple of days. They didn't take a line, and then they left. Boro Radic's group and Jovo Ostojic's group, Serb volunteer group, fought with your troops, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in which area? They did not fight side by side with us. I accept that the only ones who fought were those who received assignments from their superiors and carried these assignments out successfully, defended the front line, stayed at the line, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your troops took the Hrasnic elevation at -- trig elevation 861 [sic], didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This was around the 9th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hresa? Hresa is not even within the tactical group or was not at that point in time. This was at the entrance towards Paliv [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Hrasnic. If we can have number 65 ter 24080.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is an article from the "Nas Glas" which is a newspaper in Vogosca municipality, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's dated the 11th and 12th of August, 1992, and the article is entitled: Elevation 681 has fallen. I'm sorry I said earlier 861. I meant 681. And in this newspaper article, Boro Radic talks about being in a fierce action with the Vogosca Brigade and the Serbian volunteers and that the elevation 681's finally fallen the day before yesterday and then you're also quoted in this article: "'We pushed them towards Barica and Kobilja Glava and they have no chance of ever coming back here,' says Miladin Trifunovic, the commander of the Vogosca Brigade, saying that 'the Serbian troops will go even further.'" And then down the bottom of the article it's a quote by Jovo Ostojic, the commander of the volunteer group: "'They offered resistance but they stood no chance. By capturing this elevation the day when the idea of the liberation of the Serbian people and the Serbian countries in this area will get realised is getting even closer. We are sending a message out to those Alija's wretched minions that they had better surrender because shall get them and punish them sooner or later,' says Jovo Ostojic commander the volunteer group." And then you're quoted again: "And another thing, the Serbian volunteers will not leave this territory until the Serbian people here have won their final victory. We are here to help but Vogosca can also be proud of their heros and yesterday those were Miladin, Minja, and Dragan." Sorry that wasn't a quote by you, that was a quote in the article. So does this refresh your memory as to whether you fought with Boro Radic's group and Jovo Ostojic's group?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just take a look at the date. August, isn't it? One time the Muslim forces took this feature from us, and then they were down there and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question was does this refresh your memory as to you fighting with Jovo Ostojic's Serb volunteers and Boro Radic's group? And that these --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to explain what things were like to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think it requires a yes or a no answer --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- you either recall it or you don't.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it, but you won't let me explain how long they were there. I said in the beginning that they were there for a few days, two or three days in Vogosca, and as soon as they had one or two wounded, I can't remember exactly, they left the line and went away from there. They didn't want to stay on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Another Serb paramilitary group, the Aco legion. Do you recall those -- that group of soldiers under the command of Aco coming to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Masses of groups came and passed by. Some stayed on for a few days and left, others left immediately. How can I know? It was the beginning of the war. I cannot remember this one -- what's he called, Legija?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, didn't you say in your statement that you gave -- in December 1992 that a group of 70 soldiers came from Vogosca and in fact that they were engaged by Mirko Krajisnik - that's Momcilo Krajisnik's brother - and that the day after they were also engaged in Vogosca by Rajko Koprivica? Do you recall saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that in my statement, and I said that these groups probably came as instructed by Rajko Koprivica and Mirko Krajisnik and their task was to be placed under the command of the Vogosca Brigade. They were there for a few days, they did not want to carry out the tasks that were given to them by the Vogosca Brigade, and then they were seen off. Where they went off to afterwards I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What about Seseljevci, paramilitary group called Vaski?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Vaso Vidovic's group. He was also known as Vaski. Do you know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaske. That group did not operate in the area of Vogosca and was not in Vogosca. They were in the area of Ilijas. Vaske's group did not operate in the area of Vogosca. They operated in the area of Ilijas. In exceptional situations they came to the area of Zuc. Once they came to Zuc under the command of major -- major - what is his name? -- the then brigade commander anyway to help us save the situation so that the Muslims could not get through. As far as I know, Vaske's units was there. I mean, I'm speaking on my own behalf. It was under the command of the Ilijas Brigade. It was within the command of the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You actually -- they actually fought alongside of you or your -- your troops at Gola Brdo which you also mentioned this morning. And you said, did you not, in a statement that you gave in December 1992 that Gola Brdo was claimed several times and so the Ilijas platoon with Vlaske and part of the Ilijas Brigade came to Gola Brdo. And you said that your men and I, meaning yourself, relieved the platoon led by Vlaske. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that's what we said and that's the way it was. Our people were exhausted from the 8th of December all the way up until the end. There was fighting all the time. Now, was it the 8th or the 5th of December, whatever, I really cannot say, but throughout December there was this fierce fighting in Gola Brdo and we lost lots of our men. They were exhausted and we asked the Ilijas Brigade for help and then this unit of Vaske's came from the Ilijas Brigade and they helped us keep Gola Brdo and we got a bit of a rest. We consolidated our ranks and we took the front line again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. So you agree that you were fighting with them.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Vaske's unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions. And may I tender the document that's on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear the witness's comment to answer regarding the citation from him on this newspaper "Nas Glas"? Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Trifunovic, to "Nas Glas"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite follow the entire text, so let us see what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quoted two parts, and then as I was reading the second quote, I -- I said that I had made a mistake and the second part wasn't a quote from the witness, it was only the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The second paragraph refers to you, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraph that starts: "Most importantly, the victory was one with no losses," that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The comment was probably correct. At the time in this area, we had a very bad position up until this day, and then we made an effort to improve our positions, and then we managed to get out of these small elevations from where visibility was better, and we thought that we were safer up there at those features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. Good morning to all. After such an exhaustive cross-examination, there are certain topics that require re-examination. Could we please have 1D6600. Can we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trifunovic, you were asked quite a bit about your targets of fire, how far away Sarajevo was, so now I'd like to ask you to take a look at this. Could you please tell us whether you can recognise what this is in this satellite image, and can you tell us what is what here? Kosevo, the Bare cemetery, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help Mr. Trifunovic now so that he could mark certain locations in this photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please circle Pretis, the factory Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stadium; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see in this image Blagovac, the Pretis factory, the blue roofs? Can you see Vogosca in this image?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my glasses are very bad, and I really cannot -- I can't quite find the road leading from the stadium towards this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's make it easier. Can you see the hills? You see the Bare cemetery, and these hills here. Could you tell us what hills these are?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please circle the Hum top, the top of the Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's an elevation here, up here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please mark Zuc and Orlic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zuc and Orlic is the plateau to the left. Actually, to the right here from Hum running all the way along this ridge towards Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please mark Hum with 1 and then 2 and 3 for the road or the line that is an indication for Orlic and Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you orientate yourself now? Could you please see where Ugorsko is, Barica? Would you be able to market separation line? In other words, how far did their area stretch and where the Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are no elevations. All this area from Hum towards Zuc and Orlic, and this is between trig points 850 and trig point 830, that's a hill, a slope, doing down towards Vogosca. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the Court Usher please assist and help the witness and activate the blue line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow us the lines where you were and who held the dominant positions.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were at trig point 830.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Very well. Now, could you please mark the separation line on the side facing Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately like this. There were no trig points here. I can only orientate myself based on the terrain. I believe this is how it went, and here at the bottom I believe this was where Pretis was. So we were along this slope towards Pretis, Hotonj, and then towards Poljine, all the way here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see Kobilja Glava and the Bare cemetery? Can you now find your bearings? I believe this is the new settlement there near Bare. Could you please extend this line all the way to the Kosevo stadium or, rather, above the Kosevo stadium. In other words, what was the area that your brigade held?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it -- our brigade held the territory from Pretis and then it separated the upper and lower parts of Hotonj and stretched all the way here to the border with Poljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please put an M on one side of the line and then an S on the other side of the line. S for Serbs and M for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also the zones. In other words, all this area left of the line, all that was under the control of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This area towards the cemetery, the Kosevo stadium, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that also relate to the tops of the hills?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. All these elevations, the highest elevation between Vogosca and Sarajevo is the Hum hill, and then the Zuc Hill, 877 trig point, and then we have trig point 850, and then down to trig point 830, which is almost in the urban area of Vogosca. This is where we stopped, at trig point 830, and then we went down this slope towards Vogosca and cut the communication between Sarajevo towards -- and Kobilja Glava. We went through the Pretis area and separated this part into the left and right areas.
