This area was under the Muslim command, and here we managed to link up with the units at Kobilja Glava or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When Ms. Sutherland asked you about where you opened fire and what artillery you used, could you tell us what targets the artillery engaged?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently the fire was open at Hum hill. In other words, trig point 877 and 830. As we lost one trig point after another, they would pull up their weapons and open fire from there and we had to return the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you see Sarajevo, the centre of town, and did you open fire on Sarajevo centre? Did you engage Sarajevo at all?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't see any part of Sarajevo, not from where our positions were. So there was no need for us to engage targets we couldn't see, but we couldn't also reach those targets, the targets that would be in the centre or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please sign and date this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to tender it. My apology to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me, please, what the date is today? The 27th; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now request 65 ter 24175, please, on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. I asked for this document because it involves your human resources, both volunteers and -- now, would you take a look at this, please.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been reading it. Please bear with me. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you're addressing Mladic directly. In other words, you were all the way pushed to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your men were exhausted, that they were bringing in fresh forces? And here it says, "We have a lot of wounded and killed. Help before it is too late." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how did these fighters get killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I mentioned a few moments ago that in December, from early December, perhaps even late November, enemy forces, in other words Muslim forces, attacked persistently this part, the general plateau of Zuc, and they pushed us all the way back to elevation or trig point 830, even beyond, and these positions were very unfavourable for us. Throughout the month, in other words, we were under attack the whole month, and we had many casualties, many people were killed, many wounded. We were -- we had a shortage of resources, of medical supplies and other supplies, so we asked for assistance from General Mladic and the Main Staff, and we said we needed help that night or it would be too late the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what did that mean, that it would be too late the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't even imagine what disaster this would have spelled had the Muslim forces pushed through and entered the Vogosca area. In my view, it would have led to chaos, and the line where we stopped was some 50 to 100 to 150 metres. Each one of these fighters had their homes in the back, in the rear, and we could not allow them to pass through because had they done that, there would be chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you have before you any such incidents where Muslim forces would have entered Serb settlements and chaos would follow? I don't mean Vogosca, but did you know about any other incidents in Cemin [phoen] or Pofalici, around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did hear about Cemin and Pofalici. There was a small Serb village. They entered this small village. There were no soldiers there. There were just older men, women, and children. They were in a forest totally cut off from the surrounding world. They entered this village, and they killed everyone they found there. In other words, there was a general slaughter, catastrophe. So this was what we had before our eyes, and since Vogosca had many more people the chaos would have been far greater, many more casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D40000, 1D40000. Unfortunately, we don't have a translation for this. I didn't even realise we would need it, but we have requested the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber who issued this document and when. Or, rather, where this document were received -- was received, and if we look at the top, we can see where it was sent from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, with no English translation, the Prosecution's a bit blind-sided as to whether they can raise an objection as to whether this is something that comes out of cross-examination or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we wait a bit more to hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see this was issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, the 3rd administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 24th of August, 1991. I'm not sure, but I believe that's 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is addressed to the military command in Hadzici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. To the command of the VGU Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To this -- personally to this Muslim -- could you read that portion out. Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's Mr. Karadzic's question about this document? He needs to put a question before he just gets the witness to read chunks of the document out. I need to know what the question is to determine whether it's an objectionable question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trifunovic, you were asked about the pay that the volunteers received. Could you tell us what this document provides for in terms of the status of the volunteers, bearing in mind that it is from the ministry of defence of Yugoslavia, that this document was issued about a year -- or, rather, half a year before the war began? Could you tell us what you find in the first, second, and third paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but the witness can answer any question put by Mr. Karadzic without -- what Mr. Karadzic is asking him to do is basically read out the first three paragraphs of this document and give his answer in relation to the question that's put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, did you know how the status of volunteers was regulated in the defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each volunteer who joins the former Yugoslavia was on a list. He was registered and listed and was paid out according to the laws that were still in force in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted with a MFI indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't put a question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- pending a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think you put any questions with respect to this document, but I don't see any problem putting this document to the witness. What is your question about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted Mr. Trifunovic to take a look at the document and then to put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, this document from 1991, does it specify the regulation -- the regulating of the rights and responsibilities of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was this still in the former Yugoslavia, and was it also applied in our parts?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe this is sufficient now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the passage relevant to the payment of the volunteers? Could you ask the witness to read out that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please read item 2.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During military service, volunteers mentioned in item 1 of these rules are to be paid in accordance with instructions on the manner of payment of conscript who were drafted in order to serve their military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, the official military gazette number 20/86, 24/89, and 16/91."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now read paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the provisions of Article 119 of the Law on All People's Defence, Official Gazette of the SFRY number 21/82 and 35/91, volunteers who are drafted in the JNA have the same rights and responsibilities as conscripts."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that as early as 1982, this issue of volunteers was actually regulated and that it was just renewed in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1991, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, because I, for instance, have a brother who was drafted by the JNA in 1991, and he enjoyed all the rights that all the other active-duty personnel enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did they -- does this mean that they were duty-bound to pay salaries to these volunteers who went to fight?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe so, because this law was still in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you familiar of a crime committed by Ostojic, Vaske or Aco, aka Legija, and their units? I know they were not under military command but did they commit any crimes in that status?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar of such crimes. As for Ostojic's detachment or whatever it was called, I wanted to see them out of my area of responsibility, because he did not wish to man the front lines or be placed under military command. He wanted no other officer in his area save for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification, but I note the date of this document seems to be 24th of November, not August. In light of the bottom part of the document. Yes. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. MFI D2449.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may have been filed in October, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I said 24th of September. If I said November, it was misspoke. 24th of September, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 1D298. And we have a translation in P1134. It's the same document, but the original in the Serbian language can be more easily read in 1D298. Thank you. As for the English version could we have P1134.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about how the prisoners why used. Is there a difference in our language between a prisoner and a prisoner of war, and what do these categories mean?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A prisoner is someone who was captured at the lines. As for -- a prisoner of war was captured at the lines, whereas a detainee or a prisoner is someone who broke the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you understood this instruction from the minister, which is P6000. Perhaps we can see it on the next page. In any case, the way you interpreted it was that when you asked for the prisoners to perform work was not in contravention of the instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at P2338. 2338 P, Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often were cease-fires agreed on, and do you know whether the prisoners performed the work required during times of truce or cease-fire or not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried in any case to fortify our lines following a retreat by Muslims. As soon as there was a lull or a cease-fire, we tried to dig in and fortify. We were aware throughout the war that we were not able to return our lost lines because of the shortage of personnel. This is what we tried to do with as little effort as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it says here to assist us in the digging of trenches, does it mean that you were digging alongside the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone dug together so that it would be done as quickly and as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D226979. It has to do with the way the authorities treated paramilitary groups, first and foremost Mr. Radic. First of all, as you mentioned on day one, that Boro Radic was well known since before the war.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did people know him?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to tell lies, but he was known as a person who engaged in certain actions such as crime, theft, et cetera. I don't know. In any case, the police were aware of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, you said he was in the Patriotic League. Who did that organisation belong to? Whose formation was it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League was a Muslim force which was set up under their law. They started taking part in the war as of 30th of April, 1991, a full year before we started participating in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We do not have this translation either, but could we please zoom it in. I'll read it out: "The Kajic family, Mato (the father) and Zeljko (the son)" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic put a question before he brings a document up on to the screen. What's the -- what's the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's related to -- it seems to be related Boro Radic. Can you not wait till we hear his question? In order to put the question, I think he needs to read out the portion. I see a problem of presenting a document not interpreted, but I think we can fairly wait to his -- to hear his question. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out the three lines out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Kajic family, Mato (the father), as well as Zeljko (the son) are to protect them."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's note: It is not clear whether they need to be protect or they're supposed to provide protection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They are threatened by Boro Radic (have a talk with him. The main man knows why. ) Convey to the main man immediately." Signed Zora.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this tell to you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Boro Radic was the kind of person who took no one into account. He only did what he liked. And for some reasons of his, he threatened these people, although I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's stop here. Do you object to this line of questioning, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Sutherland. Did you say no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. I said no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a part missing. What does it say following Kajic? They need to protect it. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "They need to be protected. They are being threatened by Boro Radic. Have a talk with him. The main man knows why. Convey this to the main man immediately. Zora."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does this document tell you? First of all, this Kajic family, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I go by their first and last names, I'd say they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what does this tell you about the civilian authorities sending this telegram vis-a-vis their protection from Boro Radic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no evidence on the record that this was sent by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was leading. Could you formulate your question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the authorities were in touch by way of coded telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was Zora 112 and who would be the main man?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this tally with how you saw the authorities as to their protection they provided to members of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can probably see that throughout my testimony. We've tried throughout, including my military command and the civilian authorities, to provide as much protection as possible to any person and family irrespective of their religious or ethnic affiliation, especially those who had no rifles and who did nothing wrong. We had people who caused trouble for us, too, and we simply wanted them out, to have as few of them as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat with your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is a matter that could have been dealt with in examination-in-chief if Mr. Karadzic wanted to bring this out. It's not something I think that stems from cross-examination, the protection of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Was it not related to the issue regarding Boro Radic? Let's continue here. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I relied on this document because there was an implication that the civilian authorities were not honest in their attempts to prosecute people who broke the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No submission at the time. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Trifunovic, for your effort and for coming here twice. Thank you for your testimony, and this concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'd like to tender this MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark this telegram for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your testimony, Mr. Trifunovic. Mr. Karadzic told you that we thank you for coming to The Hague twice to give it. Now you are free to go. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. West will be leading the next witness, so we'll need one minute to swap places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we rise for five minutes in order to prepare for the next witness? Five minutes. --- Break taken at 12.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, may I request a 90(E) warning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution, the accused, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I said "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question, but in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used in evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D6252 in e-court. There's an English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, did you give a statement to my Defence team, and do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I did give a statement, and I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something, and I have to remind myself of the fact that we need to pause between question and answer in order not to exhaust the interpreters and also in order not to omit something important. So please bear that in mind. Thank you. Now, does this statement reflect everything that you could have said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, this statement that I gave does reflect everything I could have said to the Defence team, bearing in mind the circumstances involved, namely that 20 years had elapsed, but basically this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it, and did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it, and I signed it in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in court as they had been put to you, would your answers be the same as those provided in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: In essence, they would be the same like in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I please tender this statement in accordance with Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic also said "and the documents," which is my queue to rise and ask for permission to add the associated exhibits to the Rule 65 ter lists. These documents hadn't been identified by our investigator when they took the original statement, but upon coming to The Hague and being proofed by Dr. Karadzic, we realised that they were necessary to the statement and that's why they weren't on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the Prosecution does not raise this issue, I have to ask Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson about the relevance of these documents, i.e., 27 documents. How are they relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think if you look, for example, in the paragraphs -- for each paragraph, for example, paragraph 16 talking about the first document, it says that it shows that large amounts of ammunition and weaponry were transported to Igman and Sarajevo, which is also relevant to why artillery was being directed at those areas. Then paragraph 17 shows that Muslim forces -- and it refers now here to the next ten documents, and it says they show that Muslim forces continually fired on the centre of Hadzici, and there were no military targets in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So pausing there, how is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's relevant for different reasons depending on the document, but as -- if you look through paragraph 16 through -- through 25 or 26, it shows the various reasons why they're relevant, to show the activity of the other side so that the shelling by the Serbs is not on -- directed at civilian objects but are directed at military targets such as paragraph 21. So it's our position that this -- should these documents show why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Take a look at paragraph 21 by way of example. This document shows that once again the target of the attacks was hospital in Blazuj. I drafted and signed this document. How is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's relevant to show the nature of the attacks that were being directed against his brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is not a tu quoque defence, how is it -- I can't -- I find it difficult to follow the logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not a tu quoque defence. Just because the Muslims were attacking civilian objects doesn't give the Serbs the right to attack civilian objects. We're not claiming it for that reason. We're claiming it to show what the conditions were under which this war was being conducted and how basically the position that his brigade found themselves in in having to respond to the kind of attacks that were being launched against the area of their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once it was raised, can I hear from you Ms. West on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't disagree with you, and I came to the same conclusion in reading it. However -- and if you look at the rest of this statement, you'll find that paragraph 6, 7, 9, 11 also fall into this same type of category. For this witness -- made the decision not to file any formal motion in -- regarding these particular paragraphs, although I think you will understand the Prosecution's position on these paragraphs when you hear the cross-examination which would be the most part not to address them at all. I again don't disagree with your comments, but I did acknowledge in going through this that the defendant authenticated each and every one of these documents. They were drafted by the witness himself, and he made some comment as to -- regarding why they in his position -- in his -- from his perspective they were important to his case. We don't agree with that, but in regards to your guidelines as to whether they're inseparable and dispensable, I think they do reach that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the course of giving testimony, I think the witness can touch upon these issues, but my question was whether we need to admit all of these voluminous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that they -- given that they corroborate the testimony of the witness and they're documents that he authored, they're not tangential documents. So I think that they should all be admitted. Also, Mr. President, this is -- the context of the war has been the basis for admitting many, many exhibits by the Prosecution and hearing a lot of evidence, including things that took place even before the war, so I don't think that it's necessary to exclude documents that were authored by this witness that are incorporated into a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, we'll receive the -- all the documents, but in the future, the Chamber will keep a closer look into the relevance and necessity of the documents. So I would expect the Defence to exercise the same caution in tendering documents, in particular in the way -- by way of revising the statement. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. We'll give the number. And what's the number for the statement itself?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the remaining associated exhibits, the numbers will be given in due course by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. Now I would like to read out the summary of Mr. Dunjic's statement in the English language. [In English] Velimir Dunjic graduated from the military academy in 1975. He discharged the following duties: Platoon commander, company commander, battalion commander, and brigade commander. In the VRS he was brigade commander. He worked in the JNA and the VRS between 1990 and April 1992, when the war broke out. In 1991, he had intelligence about the preparations of the Green Berets at Mount Igman and about the meetings of the Patriotic League in Sokolovic Kolonija. During this time he also obtained information about the preparations to liquidate him by members of the SDA, a taxi driver and a driver from the city transport company Gras. The State Security Service removed his son from Sarajevo because of fear the SDA might kidnap him to blackmail him. When the SDA issued instructions to Muslims not to do their compulsory military service in the units of the JNA, he received the approval from the corps commander General Djurdjevac to mobilise volunteers who wanted to receive training and be in the reserve, and he hand-picked and personally trained the future members of the reserve crews. Velimir Dunjic was in the VRS from August or September 1992 to January 1993 as commander of the Igman Brigade. There were no incidents with the Croats, but there were daily armed provocations and attacks from the Muslim forces. The task of the Muslim Special Police Units and Juka Prazina's paramilitary units was to cut off his units' defence in Sarajevo which would, in turn, cause the fall of the whole area which was inhabited by tens of thousands of Serbs living on their hearths. The zone of the brigade did not change significantly other than the liberation of Doglodi and Azici after repelling the attacks of Muslim paramilitary and police units and the liberation of Otis later on. The Muslim attack on Doglodi left six civilian casualties. The deployment of the units of the brigade under his command did not allow for the possibility of sniper fire. He received information about numerous Serbian civilians and soldiers killed by Muslim snipers in the areas of Nedzarici, Rajlovac, Vogosca and along the road linking the area to Pale. In January 1993, three Serbian soldiers were killed when the positions of the Rajlovac Battalion were attacked from the Breza-Rakovica axis. The attack was stopped, thus thwarting the Muslim operation. After that and the incident with General Galic, he acted in accordance with the written orders of the Supreme Command on his dismissal and left the VRS with which he had no more contact whatsoever. In 1994, he left the VJ, Army of Yugoslavia, also. UN members and various humanitarian convoys passed through his unit's zone of responsibility and UN aircrafts flew over it, bringing humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. It was a well-known fact that Muslim units would launch attack two or three days after an aircraft carrying humanitarian aid landed or following the passage of humanitarian convoys, which allowed them to infer that those were being used to bring ammunition and weapons to the Muslim units. This was further established when ammunition was found in the false bottom of the truck on two occasions at check-points controlled by Serbian forces, and gunpowder was found in medical oxygen tanks. His unit did not commit any crime in contradiction to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions while he was in command. Measures taken by him against members of his unit involved criminal reports against soldiers for desertion and for selling infantry ammunition through Kiseljak. In 1992, UN Polish forces were escorting over 100 men of Afro-Asian origin, all of whom were weight-lifting champions and agreed between -- aged between 20 and 30 who were leaving Sarajevo in the direction of Tarcin. The explanation they gave was that the men were students who came to Sarajevo to study. Supreme Command gave orders to allow them to leave in spite of the fact that it was clear that they were well-prepared and trained soldiers. [Interpretation] For the time being, I won't have any questions for Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have I missed something, Mr. Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Maybe there's something in the translation. First of all, as far as the attack is concerned, this is Christmas 1993. It wasn't the Rajlovac Battalion that was attacked, it was the Rakovac Battalion that was attacked. That's one thing. Perhaps it's a misinterpretation. And secondly, it's not that these Afro-Asians were prize weight-lifters. It was this Polish person who led them. He was a world champion in that field. I think I said that accurately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is just a mistake in the summary, but in the statement that is clearly stated. I can now let Ms. West deal with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put down your headphone for the moment. Mr. Karadzic, I have difficulty understanding the first two sentences in para 8, which says: "I didn't have snipers in my brigade. The deployment of units of the brigade under my command did not allow for the possibility of sniper fire from the positions of the warring sides." I don't know what it means. Could you put that to the witness, live if necessary, and then we'll have a break. Could the usher kindly ask the witness to wear the -- yes. He understood my body language already. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, in relation to snipers in your brigade, you speak about that in paragraph 8. How come it was not possible to use them because of the positions? Can you explain that a bit?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I can. I mentioned in my statement that both warring sides, that is to say our side and the Muslim side, the positions did not make it possible for snipers to operate. The positions were below Igman toward Ormanj, towards Velezenik Kokorska [phoen]. So these were not urban areas. Those were the positions that I held, and I think I state this correctly in my statement. The Muslims did not open sniper fire at my soldiers in my area of responsibility either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can show this to us on the map, can you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I think I can understand the -- the sentence. Are you happy with these explanations, Ms. West? Can we go along with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a break now for half an hour and resume at five past 1.00 -- or I'm sorry, 45 minutes. So we'll resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dunjic. As you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. In your statement, at paragraph 1 you indicate that you were the commander of the Igman Brigade from August 1992 to January 1993. Can you tell us exactly what date in August you became the commander, please?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: As I stated, in August or September, as far as I could recall, that's when I was appointed, but the exact date was the 4th of September, 1992, when I was appointed to the post of commander of the Igman Brigade. I took the liberty of bringing with me an excerpt from records of the VRS, which is also stamped, where -- and certified where what I've just said can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it. That was the 4th of September, 1992. I also understand from the first paragraph that you were dismissed in 1993, in January of 1993, and you went to -- went and joined the VJ. As regards your dismissal in January of 1993 from the SRK, that was involuntary; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us the circumstances of your dismissal.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a systemic disagreement between me and the corps commander, and also there were some differences between us, which is why I received an order whereby I was dismissed from the post of brigade commander. I would like to add that on two occasions I sent some communications to the Main Staff, and I even requested one time to be relieved of duty. This was sometime in November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You were requested to be relieved of duty. That's not in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, it's not in my statement. I recalled it later, later on, but you can check this information because it had been sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you just described the circumstances of your dismissal as differences that you had between yourself and the SRK corps command. Tell us what those differences were.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, these were systemic differences. There were differences in the approach to the organisation of the army and the fighting itself, but there was also a personal rift between me and General Galic, and that was actually the final straw. Now, because of my respect or dignity to preserve the dignity of General Galic's -- perhaps we could move to closed or private session so that I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We don't need to do that now. If we do, we'll do that later, but let's just move on. Was the nature of your dismissal in January known to the VJ when you joined them in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it probably was, because I remained in the Army of -- in the Army of Yugoslavia up until June 1994 sometime when at my request I left the JNA. So I wasn't dismissed. I left it on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was there any delay in the process of you joining the VJ because of the unfavourable nature of your dismissal from the SRK?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you require any references in order to be accepted by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, there probably were references, but I really wouldn't know because the principle of the reappointments where there would also be an assessment, a job performance evaluation, that would not have gone through me. It would have been sent through other channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, from September of 1992 through January of 1993, during your reign, there was activity, military activity, at Zuc; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was fighting on Zuc. However, Zuc was outside of the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And specifically in December of 1992, the ABiH was able to regain control of Zuc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you went to that area of conflict in December of 1992 even though it was outside your area of responsibility, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I failed to mention in my statement that -- and my apologies if I am wrong about the exact dates, but sometime in November, in late November, the corps command, after the death of Mr. Zoran Borovina, who was the commander of the Ilidza Brigade and my deputy, and after certain unfavourable circumstances in Rajlovac, I was appointed to be the commander over these three brigades, the Rajlovac, the Igman, and the Ilidza Brigades. And I apologise once again for having omitted this detail, because as I looked at these documents that actually jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that's a pretty big detail, you would agree; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you will understand that over 20 years have passed since I left that area and that as of 1994, I was not involved in any of this any more. I was not in the military any more. I started a completely new chapter, as it were, and I wanted also to put this behind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So the Trial Chamber has heard evidence even today regarding the events at Zuc. Can you tell us who was it that ordered you to go to Zuc? And now I'm talking about December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't at Zuc itself. I was in the foothills of Zuc, in the general direction of Rajlovac. So there was the Rajlovac Brigade there deployed, and then there was the Vogosca Brigade. They linked up at Mijatovica Kosa, a slope to the north of Sokolje, and I had a problem there because the lines had collapsed as far as the Rajlovac Brigade was concerned. I managed to recapture those lines once and then the second time. So that's where I was actually active, not on Zuc itself, because that was held by the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's focus again on my question and it was who ordered you to be, and you say, at the foothills of Zuc. Can you give me the name of a person?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I received a written order from the Chief of Staff of the corps, Colonel Dragan Marcetic, to the effect that I was the co-ordinator over these three brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was your task in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: The task in December 1992 was to prevent the fall of Rajlovac. If Rajlovac fell, all six north-western municipalities where the Army of Republika Srpska was deployed, and there were tens of thousands of civilians, would have fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 of your statement, you indicated that Brne Gavrilovic's unit was in your zone. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, do you have your written statement with you? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention to paragraph 13 of your statement. That's the part where you spoke about Brne Gavrilovic's unit, and that's where you said: [As read] "Among the units which were in the zone when I came was also the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic. After a while, it was also -- it also put itself under the brigade command and did not commit any crimes in contradiction to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions while I was in command." Notwithstanding what you have in there, were you aware of his unit's reputation, his unit's nefarious reputation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the units and the situation within the units as they were, I found them as they were. Now, I don't know whether you're aware, but pursuant to a decision of the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska, in the second half of 1992 the status of volunteers and units within the VRS was assessed, and it was concluded that volunteers did not have the attribute or the status of paramilitaries, but, rather, that they were members of the VRS, legal and legitimate; the only difference being in the way they joined. Now, their tasks and responsibilities were the same as those of all the other members of the VRS. So that was the first decision taken by the Supreme Court of the -- of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic, and we're going to spend a bit of time speaking about the paramilitaries. But my question for you, and please listen to my question and try to be responsive if you can, is when you came in in September of 1992, were you aware of Brne Gavrilovic's reputation, the reputation of his unit?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of their reputation. However, we are now actually moving to the area of ideological differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, we're not. Thank you, Mr. Dunjic. No, we're not.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my next question for you, Mr. Dunjic, regards that specific reputation. If we could have D01080, please, and this is a MUP report in June of 1992. If we can have page 3 of the English and page 3 of the Cyrillic. This is June 1992. So this is in the period of time just before you came in. And on page 3 there's a paragraph, and I want to share some of the information in here with you. On page 3 of the Cyrillic, it's the second full paragraph. And the paragraph beginning with "In addition": "... the citizens complained to the Serbian public security station Ilidza reporting thefts and forceful expelling of Muslim citizens from Ilidza committed by Seselj's men." Now, were you aware that Gavrilovic had been appointed by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all I was not aware of that, and secondly, we are talking about June. But you agreed with me that I was appointed as brigade commander on the 4th of September, which is a few months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Exactly. And what I'd like to know is when it appears that in the summer before you came on that citizens in Ilidza were complaining about Seselj's men, did these complaints ever reach your ears when you got there in September?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many people were in his unit when you took -- when you came in September?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you will understand that I don't know the exact number of men, but I believe it was around 80 or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next sentence is: [As read] "However, when the Serbian public security station Ilidza decided that in such cases interventions were necessary, the president of Crisis Staff of Ilidza, Nedeljko Prstojevic and his deputy opposed this decision stressing that with Seselj's men there should be no messing around." In other words, they were doing it on their behalf, since Prstojevic and his deputy tasked them with it. Mr. Dunjic, did you know Nedeljko Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please just have something clarified? Do these Seselj's men, is that a reference to Brne because it doesn't say so here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the subject -- yes. Let us clarify that with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness is able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic did you hear that question? Do you know if -- as regards Seselj's men, if that refers to Brne Gavrilovic and his men?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say this: I knew Mr. Brnovic [as interpreted] when I arrived there, when I was appointed commander of the brigade because he was president of the municipality in Ilidza. And at that time I wasn't really interested in the ideological differences, whether someone was a member of the Radical Party or of the Communist Party of Republika Srpska or the SDS. I didn't care about that. What I wanted -- all I was concerned with was my fighters who were to obey my orders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just help here. I believe that the witness said that he did not know that Brne was appointed by Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me just make a clarification. At line 13, you said: Let me just say that I knew this person when I arrived there when I was appointed commander of the brigade. Did you say Mr. Prstojevic you knew when you arrived there or Mr. Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you were asking about Prstojevic and I told you that I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you knew him before you arrived in September?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I did know Prstojevic. I had known him while I was -- well, I knew him from when I was the battalion commander in Lukavica in 1991. That's when we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And during the winter -- excuse me, the fall and winter of 1992-1993, did you speak to Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. When was the last time you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe just before I left, because he offered that they organise a send-off party for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this would be 1993.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's last time you've ever had a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that we talked again, maybe some 15, 16, or 17 years later. It is possible that we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Mr. Prstojevic and Seselj's men in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, again you're asking about things that happened before I was there and things that were outside of the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, do you have your statement, para 13 in front of you? It reads like this: "Among the units which were in the zone when I came was also the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic. After a while it also put itself under the brigade command and it did not commit any crimes ..." To me it sounds as if they had committed crime before they put themselves under your command. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know, but I stated in my statement that they did not commit any crimes while I was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it to you, Ms. West. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Ms. West speak into the microphone that is in front of her, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And we were just talking about the relationship between Mr. Prstojevic and Seselj's men in Ilidza, and you said that you didn't know about that because it was things that happened before you were there. May we have P2302. Let me now ask you about the relationship between Mr. Prstojevic and Branislav Gavrilovic, the gentleman who was in your unit. And you're going to see a document in front of you and it's dated a few months before you get there. I'll tell you it's dated in July. However, it has to do with the housing of Gavrilovic and his unit, and it's a signed document from Mr. Prstojevic, and he says: [As read] "It is hereby approved to use the motel facility in Gladno Polje and the deserted summer houses in the vicinity for the needs of the Serbian volunteer units from the lines of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza MUP. "The commander of all Serbian Autonomous District Romanija volunteer units, Branislav Gavrilovic, will be conducting admission and training of Serbian volunteers arriving to this area." So, sir, my question for you is when you came in September 1992 and Gavrilovic and his unit were under your command, were they still being housed through the offer of Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, from the document that you've shown me, my only conclusion would be that Mr. Prstojevic and Mr. Gavrilovic had a good relationship, and my answer to your question would be, yes, they were still housed in the same facilities as described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In your role as commander of Gavrilovic and his men, you gave them orders and they performed them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Within my brigade, I had between 2.500 and 3.000 men. Gavrilovic's unit numbered 800. And I wasn't Gavrilovic's commander. I was the brigade commander. His unit was part of the brigade. All of the units carried out my orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'll take that as a yes. And my next question is: If Gavrilovic's unit performed some action during this period of time that his unit was in your command, shall we assume that this action was the result of a task ordered by you and your chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Either I'm not receiving appropriate interpretation, or I misunderstand the question. They were not outside the chain of command. It was a unit which carried out orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't say they were outside of the chain of command, but I think I understand that it's your testimony that they were within your brigade, and they took orders under your chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if they were committing illegal acts, you would know that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I had 3.000 soldiers or between 2.500 and 3.000. If I had known of such things, I would have treated it much the same way in cases of soldiers when I submitted criminal reports and dozens. I would go by the information received from the security organs and from the members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we have P02296, and we're going to go to paragraph 74. I know you said earlier that you were unaware of Mr. Gavrilovic's reputation and his unit's reputation, but you -- and you clarified that you didn't know this coming in, but now I'd like to look at a period of time in the fall of 1992 when you were the actual brigade commander. And this is a statement from Tihomir Glavas, who was the chief of the Ilidza SJB at the same time that you were there, and in paragraph 74 he speaks about this particular group. And at paragraph 74, he says: [As read] "The local group of Seseljevci was led by Branislav Gavrilovic, called Brne. I personally had problems with this group because he was operating in Ilidza when I came. His headquarters was in an orchard ... directives from military, political and police ministry ordered that these paramilitary forces be subordinated to military commands or be disbanded and even liquidated if they refused. Gavrilovic's unit was involved in crimes on our territory, thefts, looting. His unit never wanted to fight in the woods or front lines. They just went to places to fight where they could steal and loot such as Otes and Doglodi. They also fought at the airport settlement next to Dobrinja." Now this is during a period of time where this gentleman is there at the same time that you're there. And could you tell us were you aware of these types of allegations against Gavrilovic's unit, these criminal allegations?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. Perhaps I can clarify something to you. As a professional soldier, I was aware of the existence of certain soldiers who are trained and ready to find -- to fight in an urban settlement, whereas there are others who were trained to fight in the mountains. Many avoided fighting in urban areas, whereas just as many avoided fighting in the mountains. As for this document, I was not aware of it. To me, it says nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't answer my question. Let's try this again. I'm not asking whether you're aware of this document. I'm asking whether you were aware of the criminal allegations at the time that you were there that were being voiced regarding Gavrilovic's unit.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, the beginning of 75: "The reason they went into these areas was to steal from houses and apartments in those areas." Were you aware of those allegations?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We move to paragraph 77. You just mentioned that his unit was under your -- under your command, and paragraph 77 this speaks to the same subject. This witness had been shown a document, and he said that this is -- in this document there was a mention of a person named Vaske, another Chetnik duke in the area of Ilijas who was prone to co-operating with the army. Therefore, he could be in conflict, "he" meaning Mr. Vaske, with Gavrilovic's unit who were opposed to any co-operation with the army. What I meant by Vaske's unit co-operating with the army, I received instructions from the police leadership that Vaske's unit accepted to be subordinated into military command and Gavrilovic refused. Mr. Dunjic, is it your testimony here today that Gavrilovic was under the military command in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have said so in the statement, and I stand by it. He was under my command in my brigade while I was at the helm of the brigade. Whatever happened before or later is something I cannot answer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At this point I'm not asking you about what happened before or later. I'm asking you about what happened while you were the commander of the brigade in September of 1992 through January of 1993. During that period of time, is it your testimony that he committed no crimes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your testimony also that you were not aware of his reputation otherwise?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You see, I keep saying that I have -- had between 2.500 and 3.000 soldiers, and the group or detachment of 80 soldiers was not my primary focus.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was the position of the SRK corps command, was it not, that paramilitaries should either be under their command or they should have to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you had had any paramilitaries within your zone but not under your command, you had a duty to inform your superiors, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You mean the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your superiors, yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You keep imputing things. I've already mentioned what the first decision of the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska was, and I abided by it. In the area of responsibility of my brigade, I had no other unit save for the detachment which I found there when I assumed my duties as commander, brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have D01076.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another MUP document, and this is coming closer to the period of time when you started in September. And if we can have page 3 of the English at the bottom and page 2 of the B/C/S, at the bottom as well. This is another document that speaks about Gavrilovic's unit. And just to say again D01076. This may be my mistake. Sir, before you came in, who was the brigade commander before you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think it was Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24197, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a document from August again, recognising this is right before you came in. This is a document from Tomislav Sipcic, and in it he's reporting on general -- the general situation within the command, and under number 4, at the end, he says: "Moreover, very little is being done to disarm paramilitary formations. The local authorities are establishing and bringing in new ones from the outside." Now, when you came in September, did you understand this to continue to be true? Did you understand it to be the case that the local political leadership were responsible for bringing in paramilitaries in your zone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I am a soldier, a professional soldier. As regards many things, I tried not to meddle with the work of the civilian authorities. You keep going back to Mr. Sipcic's order. I was not there at the time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you told us that you spoke to Mr. Prstojevic quite often, and I understand in the fall and winter of 1992, you at least worked with him for a period of time. In the course of that relationship, did you understand that the local political leadership had been responsible for bringing in paramilitaries and were bringing in more?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility that I had there were no other units except for the one I found there. I repeat, I did speak with Mr. Prstojevic as I did with all other municipal representatives in that part of Sarajevo, but it all had to do with providing security and securing logistics for the army like food, boots, burials of soldiers and civilians, and taking care of their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But as I understand your testimony today, part of the army you purport to be is Mr. Gavrilovic's unit, and so if Mr. Prstojevic then had some connection with Gavrilovic's unit, which -- would you agree some would have considered to be a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Now you're asking for my opinion. You have shown me a document where Prstojevic on one hand secured accommodation for him, and on the other he said that he had issues with Gavrilovic. I'm not familiar with the nature of their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know if Prstojevic had any role in bringing Seselj's men to the area?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, I don't know of such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: And he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So either you don't know of it or he did not. Please clarify your answer.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: As regards my area of responsibility while I commanded the brigade, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And as regards to that area of responsibility while you commanded the brigade, are you aware of whether the republican level political leadership had a role in bringing in paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what about before you came? Are you aware of that leadership bringing in paramilitaries before you came to that area?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was at the other end of the theatre. I wasn't even in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P02228, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an April 1992 conversation between Seselj and Gavrilovic. We won't read the whole thing, but towards the bottom of the English Gavrilovic says: "Everything's fine." And then Seselj says: "Look, I've just called Pale. I can't find Radovan and nobody can find him. Brne: "Yeah. Seselj: "But I left a message that if they didn't get our men out, we'll withdraw all our men from the front lines and we'll never deploy them again." Would you agree with me that at least from that very short part that I read to you that Seselj is directing a complaint regarding his men to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You're obviously trying to suggest an answer. I keep saying that I was not in the area at all at the time of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's go to the time when you were there in September of 1992 and on. When you were in command of Brne and his men, what role did Seselj take as to their deployment or task?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, he had no role to play.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: By September of 1992 through the time that you left in January of 1993 or ordered to leave, Galic was the commander of the SRK; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P05060, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is written on September 12th, so this is when you were already in command, and it regards a meeting. And this is a Galic document, and we're going to go to number 3 in both documents. And he's talking about a meeting that he had with the SRK command, brigade commanders, presidents of Municipal Assemblies, head of the military departments and members of the General Staff. Now, he had this meeting on September 6, and you came into brigade command, as I understand it, September 4th. Do you remember attending a meeting a few days after you started?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I don't, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And number 3 and speaking about this meeting, he says that -- that they should secure absolute concordance and unity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we find the part in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Pardon me. It's number 3. It's page 1. There we go. It's towards the bottom of both.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it says: "Secure absolute concordance and unity at all levels with civilian authorities and MUP forces and eliminate any creation of paramilitary and parapolitical and not allow any conflicts, because we have a common goal." So when you came in in September, you were well aware that it was Galic's position that there should be no paramilitaries within the VRS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 65 ter 24198, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to skip ahead a few months to see whether this position changed or remained the same. We'll now go to October 19th. This is another Galic document, and we're looking under paragraph 4, and it's the part that's underlined. It's under "Morale": "There are again incidences of bringing in paramilitary groups and units from the outside under the guise of volunteer units. Having learned from previous experience, we believe that these groups will have a very negative influence on the morale of the soldiers and the population." Sir, what was the view at the time as to why the paramilitaries were a negative influence?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what other people thought, but I had no paramilitary units in my brigade. The only unit that I found there was quickly put under my command. I wasn't interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But can you tell us in a general way because you are there at the time, you're attending these meetings, you had to be aware that there was a general notion that the paramilitaries had a negative influence. Tell us what you understood the negative influence to be.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to finish my answer when I mentioned the JNA. Perhaps it would have been clearer. If you want a contextual explanation regarding your question, I'd be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only if giving a contextual explanation will tell us what the negative influence was. Can you do that? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: You are suggesting an answer. I'm telling you that paramilitary units, in the heads of many officers of the former JNA, were paramilitary only because they were called Vucjak, wolves, and other names. By the same analogy, the Deltas and the Seals are also paramilitary formations. Those how those people reasoned, due to ideological differences, whereas I was not interested in any ideological differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I've given you the opportunity to give us some context here but we still haven't answered the question. Would you agree with me that at the time other people thought the paramilitaries were a negative influence but it appears that you did not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No. No. I agree that that's what other people thought, but that was for ideological reasons, in their minds, which were something I couldn't comprehend.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P0230, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is a November 1992 document from Galic. It's a regular combat report, November 18th. And under number 3 at the bottom of the English and bottom of the B/C/S, it's written: "The situation in the territory without significant changes. However, a paramilitary formation consisting of about 25 men commanded by Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, is active in the Rakovica sector. This is a group of criminals whose behaviour is damaging the reputation of the Republika Srpska Army in the eyes of the population in this territory." Now, this is already in November of 1992, and their reputation continues on. Their nefarious reputation continues on. By November were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can comment upon your ignorance. I mentioned before that there were 80 of them, whereas here we have 25. There was an obvious numerical difference save for some general remarks on the negative influences which arose only due to ideological reasons. If you showed me proof that this or that person from that -- this or that unit did this or that, then I can comment, and if -- had there been such cases, I would have reported them. I would have issued criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So as I understand it, it's your position that at the time you weren't aware of this and you've repeated a few times that there were only 80 men in his unit, yet there was 2.500 to 3.000 men in the entire brigade, suggesting that there might be a reason why you would not have known, but in this case the corps commander knows, somebody who is well above you and who is looking after far more people. Why do you think he knows about this reputation yet you didn't?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about someone's reputation. That's like assessments of ice skating where you say artistic impression. Well, there was nothing specific that anyone would have come up to me with so that I could take certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was your support of Brne's unit also supported by the local authorities? Specifically I'm speaking about Nedeljko Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just intervene in the transcript? Mr. Dunjic said, "I didn't see any evidence that an act, a criminal act, had been committed." So that portion did not make it into the transcript in his previous reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Were you aware -- was Brne's unit also supported by the local civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
